entities.name: twelve-tone technique
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The twelve-tone technique, developed by Austrian composer Arnold Schoenberg in the early 20th century, revolutionized the landscape of Western classical music. Emerging around 1923, this method of composition employs all twelve notes of the chromatic scale with equal importance, eschewing traditional tonal hierarchies. Schoenberg's innovation not only marked a departure from the prevailing diatonic systems but also represented a broader cultural shift towards modernism, reflecting the tumultuous social and political climate of post-World War I Europe.

Schoenberg's twelve-tone method was outlined in his 1923 composition 'Suite for Piano, Op. 25', which served as a seminal text for composers seeking to explore atonality. This technique involves the creation of a tone row, a specific sequence of the twelve pitches, which serves as the foundation for developing musical material throughout the piece. The technique gained prominence and was further expanded by Schoenberg's students, including Alban Berg and Anton Webern, who contributed to the Second Viennese School, a group that played a pivotal role in shaping contemporary music practices.

The legacy of the twelve-tone technique extends far beyond Schoenberg's immediate circle; it fundamentally altered the trajectory of music composition, leading to the development of serialism and influencing a wide range of genres, from avant-garde to film scores. By the mid-20th century, composers such as Pierre Boulez and Milton Babbitt embraced and expanded upon Schoenberg’s principles, integrating them into their own works. As a cultural footprint, the twelve-tone technique exemplifies the struggle for artistic freedom and innovation amid the uncertainties of modern life, encapsulated in Schoenberg’s assertion that, 'The composer must be a soldier in the battle for the spirit of mankind.'
